lessons.title: Optimal Planting Dates and Spacing
lessons.body:
In Africa, cabbage can be grown year-round in cooler highland areas, but timing is critical in warmer regions. Aim to plant at the start of the rains or when temperatures are between 15Â°C and 20Â°C. In Kenya's highlands, plant in March-April and September-October. In Nigeria's Jos Plateau, plant from April to June and September to November. Avoid planting in extreme heat (above 30Â°C) as heads become loose and bitter. If you have irrigation, you can plant in dry seasons but expect more pest pressure.

Spacing determines head size and yield. For most varieties, use 60 cm between rows and 45 cm between plants. This gives about 37,000 plants per hectare. For smaller heads, tighten to 45 cm x 30 cm (about 74,000 plants/ha). For larger heads, widen to 75 cm x 60 cm (about 22,000 plants/ha). In raised beds, plant in double rows 60 cm apart, with 45 cm between plants in the row, and 90 cm between bed centers.

Always plant on raised beds or ridges, especially in heavy rain areas. Beds should be 20-30 cm high and 1 m wide. This prevents waterlogging and root diseases. If you are in a dry area, plant in furrows or flat beds to conserve moisture. Mark your spacing with a measuring stick or string to keep uniform. Uniform spacing makes weeding, spraying, and harvesting easier.

Before planting, ensure your soil is well-prepared with compost or manure. Apply 2-3 handfuls of well-rotted manure per planting hole. Mix it well with soil. Water the holes before planting. Plant seedlings in the evening or on a cloudy day to reduce transplant shock. After planting, water immediately. If you plant too close, you get small heads and more disease. Too far apart, you waste land and get sunburn on heads. So stick to recommended spacing for your variety and market.

lessons.title: Planting Depth and Seedling Handling
lessons.body:
Cabbage seedlings are delicate. The depth you plant them at can make or break your crop. The rule is simple: plant the seedling so that the first true leaves are just above the soil surface. The root ball should be covered, but the growing point (where new leaves emerge) must not be buried. If you bury the growing point, the plant will rot or produce a deformed head. If you plant too shallow, roots dry out and the seedling falls over.

When transplanting, handle seedlings by the leaves, not the stem. The stem is easily crushed, and a damaged stem means a dead plant. Use a small trowel or a stick to make a hole deep enough to take the entire root ball. Place the seedling in the hole, then firm the soil around it gently with your hands. Do not press too hardâyou want the soil to be firm but not compacted. Water immediately after planting to settle the soil around the roots.

Seedlings should be 4-6 weeks old when transplanted. They should have 4-5 true leaves and be about 10-15 cm tall. If you buy seedlings from a nursery, check that they are healthy, stocky, and free of pests. Avoid seedlings with yellow leaves or thin, stretched stems. Before transplanting, water the nursery bed thoroughly so the soil sticks to the roots. This reduces root damage when you lift the seedlings.

If you are planting in hot weather, transplant in the late afternoon or evening. If it is very sunny, provide shade for the first 2-3 days using palm fronds or shade nets. In the first week after transplanting, water twice dailyâmorning and eveningâunless it rains. After one week, reduce to once daily. This helps the seedlings establish quickly. A well-planted seedling will start growing within 3-4 days. If you see wilting after 5 days, check for root damage or pests.

lessons.title: Row Arrangement and Plant Density
lessons.body:
How you arrange your cabbage plants in the field affects airflow, sunlight, and disease pressure. The most common arrangement is single rows on raised beds. Rows should run in the direction of the prevailing wind to improve air movement and reduce fungal diseases. In flat beds, use a north-south orientation if possible, so both sides of the row get sunlight. In Africa, many farmers use ridges or beds, so rows follow the bed direction.

Plant density is the number of plants per unit area. For cabbage, the recommended density varies with variety and market. For standard varieties like Gloria F1 or Copenhagen Market, aim for 35,000 to 40,000 plants per hectare. This means spacing of 60 cm between rows and 45 cm between plants. For compact varieties like Green Boy, you can go up to 50,000 plants per hectare with 50 cm x 40 cm spacing. For large heads for restaurants, reduce to 25,000 plants per hectare with 75 cm x 60 cm.

Higher density gives more heads per hectare but smaller heads and more disease because of poor airflow. Lower density gives larger heads but fewer of them, and you may get sunburn on exposed heads. The key is to match density to your market. If you sell to supermarkets that want 1-1.5 kg heads, use medium density. If you sell to local markets that accept smaller heads, you can plant denser.

In double-row beds, plant two rows 45 cm apart on a 1 m wide bed, with 45 cm between plants in the row, and 75 cm between bed centers. This gives about 40,000 plants per hectare. Always leave paths every 10-15 meters for access. After planting, draw a simple map of your field showing rows and beds. This helps you plan weeding, spraying, and harvesting. Remember, overcrowding stresses plants and invites pests like aphids and diamondback moth.

lessons.title: Mulching Techniques for Cabbage
lessons.body:
Mulching is covering the soil around your cabbage plants with a layer of material. It conserves moisture, suppresses weeds, and keeps the soil cool. In Africa, you can use organic mulches like dry grass, straw, banana leaves, or maize stover. Spread a layer 5-10 cm thick around the plants, but keep it 5 cm away from the stem to prevent rot. You can also use plastic mulch, which is more expensive but lasts longer and warms the soil in cool highlands.

Organic mulches are cheap and easy to find. After planting, wait until the seedlings are established (about 2 weeks), then spread mulch. Dry grass is excellentâmake sure it has no seeds, or you will introduce weeds. Banana leaves are good but break down quickly. Maize stover is durable but may harbor pests like stem borers; chop it finely. In dry areas, a thick mulch of 10 cm can reduce watering by half. In wet areas, a thinner mulch of 5 cm is enough to suppress weeds.

Plastic mulch comes in rolls, usually black or silver. Black plastic warms the soil and controls weeds completely. Silver plastic reflects sunlight and repels aphids and thrips. To use plastic mulch, lay it on the bed before planting, secure the edges with soil, and cut holes for your seedlings. It costs more but saves labor on weeding and can increase yields by 20-30%. In South Africa and Kenya, many commercial cabbage farmers use plastic mulch.

Mulching also prevents soil splash on leaves, which reduces soil-borne diseases like black rot. It keeps heads clean, so you get a better market price. If you use organic mulch, add more as it decomposes. Do not use fresh manure as mulchâit burns plants and attracts flies. After harvest, you can plow organic mulch into the soil to improve organic matter. For plastic mulch, remove and dispose of it properly, or reuse it for the next season if intact. Mulching is one of the cheapest ways to improve cabbage production.

lessons.title: Irrigation Setup After Planting
lessons.body:
Cabbage needs consistent moisture, especially in the first 3 weeks after transplanting. A good irrigation setup ensures you can water evenly and efficiently. The simplest method is a watering can, but for more than 0.5 hectare, you need a better system. Drip irrigation is the best for cabbage because it saves water, reduces weeds, and keeps leaves dry, which prevents fungal diseases. A drip kit for 1 hectare costs about $500-$1000, but you can start with a smaller kit for 0.2 hectare.

If you cannot afford drip, use furrow irrigation. Make furrows between your beds, and let water flow gently. Do not flood the bedsâwater should reach the root zone, not the leaves. In sandy soil, water more often but less amount. In clay soil, water less often but more amount. A general rule: cabbage needs 25-30 mm of water per week. In hot weather, it may need 40 mm. Check soil moisture by digging 10 cm deepâif it feels dry, irrigate.

For overhead irrigation, use sprinklers but water early in the morning so leaves dry before evening. Wet leaves at night invite downy mildew and black rot. If you use a hose, water at the base of the plant. After planting, water immediately, then every 2-3 days for the first week. After 2 weeks, water twice a week if no rain. During head formation, do not let the soil dry out, or heads will crack. Mulching helps retain moisture, so you can water less.

Set up your irrigation system before planting so you can water immediately after transplanting. For drip, lay lines along the rows, with emitters 30 cm apart. Connect to a water source and a filter. Test the system for even flow. For furrow, ensure a gentle slope so water reaches the end without pooling. Always have a backup planâa tank or drum for emergency watering. In dry seasons, irrigation is the difference between a good harvest and crop failure. Keep your system clean and repair leaks promptly.

lessons.title: Protecting Seedlings from Pests and Weather
lessons.body:
Young cabbage seedlings are vulnerable to pests and harsh weather. The most common pests are cutworms, aphids, diamondback moth, and flea beetles. Cutworms cut the stem at ground level. To control them, put a collar of cardboard or plastic around the stem, or sprinkle wood ash around the base. Aphids and flea beetles suck sap and transmit diseases. Spray with neem oil (5 ml per liter of water) every 7 days, or use soapy water (1 tablespoon liquid soap per liter). For diamondback moth, handpick caterpillars or spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), a natural bacteria that kills only caterpillars.

Weather extremes can also kill seedlings. Heavy rain can wash away seeds or bury small plants. If you expect heavy rain, plant on raised beds and make drainage channels. Strong sun can scorch leaves. Use shade nets (50% shade) for the first week, or plant in the shade of taller crops like maize. In cold highlands, frost can kill seedlings. Cover plants with dry grass or plastic tunnels at night. In hot lowlands, plant early in the season or use mulch to keep soil cool.

You can also use physical barriers. A row cover (agro-net) over seedlings keeps out insects and birds. It is cheap and reusable. For birds, scarecrows or reflective tape work. For snails and slugs, sprinkle ash or crushed eggshells around the bed. Check your crop every morning for signs of damage. Early detection is key. If you see holes in leaves, look for caterpillars. If leaves are curling, look for aphids underneath.

Always keep the area around your seedbed clean. Remove weeds and crop debris, as they harbor pests. Rotate cropsâdo not plant cabbage where you grew cabbage or other brassicas last season. If you use chemicals, choose those recommended for cabbage and follow the label. But start with natural methods first. A healthy seedling that is well-watered and mulched can withstand some pest damage. Your goal is to get the plants past the first 3 weeks, after which they become stronger and more resistant.

quiz.q: What is the optimal temperature range for cabbage planting?
quiz.explanation: Cabbage grows best in cool temperatures between 15Â°C and 20Â°C; extreme heat causes loose, bitter heads.

quiz.q: In Kenya's highlands, which months are recommended for planting cabbage?
options: D) Any month of the year
quiz.explanation: The highlands have two rainy seasons, making March-April and September-October ideal for cabbage planting.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for standard cabbage varieties?
quiz.explanation: 60 cm between rows and 45 cm between plants is the standard spacing for most cabbage varieties.

quiz.q: Why should cabbage be planted on raised beds in heavy rain areas?
options: B) To prevent waterlogging and root diseases
quiz.explanation: Raised beds allow excess water to drain, preventing waterlogged roots and diseases like root rot.

quiz.q: How many plants per hectare does a spacing of 60 cm x 45 cm give?
quiz.explanation: 60 cm x 45 cm spacing results in approximately 37,000 plants per hectare.

quiz.q: When transplanting cabbage seedlings, how deep should you plant them?
options: B) Just cover the root ball, leaving first true leaves above soil
C) Plant only the roots with stem exposed
quiz.explanation: The root ball should be covered, but the growing point must remain above soil to avoid rot.

quiz.q: How should you handle cabbage seedlings during transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Handling by the leaves prevents crushing the delicate stem, which can kill the plant.

quiz.q: What is the ideal age of cabbage seedlings for transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Seedlings are ready to transplant at 4-6 weeks old, when they have 4-5 true leaves.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after transplanting cabbage seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Watering immediately after planting settles the soil around the roots and reduces transplant shock.

quiz.q: In hot weather, what is the best time to transplant cabbage seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Transplanting in the late afternoon or evening reduces heat stress and water loss.

quiz.q: Why should cabbage rows run in the direction of the prevailing wind?
options: A) To improve airflow and reduce fungal diseases
quiz.explanation: Good airflow helps dry leaves and reduces fungal disease pressure.

quiz.q: What is the recommended plant density for large cabbage heads for restaurants?
quiz.explanation: Lower density (e.g., 25,000 plants/ha) allows plants to grow larger heads.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of high plant density in cabbage?
options: B) More disease due to poor airflow
quiz.explanation: Overcrowding reduces airflow, increasing humidity and disease risk.

quiz.q: In double-row beds, what is the typical spacing between bed centers?
quiz.explanation: For double-row beds, 75 cm between bed centers is common to allow access and airflow.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of mulching cabbage?
options: B) Conserves moisture and suppresses weeds
quiz.explanation: Mulch retains soil moisture, reduces weeds, and keeps soil temperature stable.

quiz.q: How thick should an organic mulch layer be around cabbage plants?
quiz.explanation: A 5-10 cm layer of organic mulch is effective for moisture retention and weed control.

quiz.q: Why should mulch be kept 5 cm away from the cabbage stem?
quiz.explanation: Mulch touching the stem can cause rot, especially in wet conditions.

quiz.q: Which type of plastic mulch repels aphids and thrips?
quiz.explanation: Silver reflective plastic mulch repels aphids and thrips by reflecting light.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using plastic mulch in cabbage farming?
options: A) It adds organic matter to soil
B) It warms soil and controls weeds
C) It is cheaper than organic mulch
quiz.explanation: Plastic mulch warms the soil in cool areas and provides excellent weed control.

quiz.q: How does mulching help reduce disease in cabbage?
options: B) By preventing soil splash on leaves
quiz.explanation: Mulch prevents soil-borne pathogens from splashing onto leaves during rain or irrigation.

quiz.q: What is the best irrigation method for cabbage to prevent fungal diseases?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation keeps leaves dry, reducing fungal disease risk and saving water.

quiz.q: How much water does cabbage need per week on average?
quiz.explanation: Cabbage requires about 25-30 mm of water per week for optimal growth.

quiz.q: When using overhead irrigation, what is the best time to water?
quiz.explanation: Watering early in the morning allows leaves to dry before evening, reducing disease.

quiz.q: What is a sign that cabbage needs irrigation?
options: B) Soil feels dry 10 cm deep
quiz.explanation: Checking soil moisture at 10 cm depth is a reliable indicator of irrigation need.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid letting soil dry out during head formation?
options: A) It causes heads to crack
quiz.explanation: Inconsistent moisture during head formation can cause heads to split or crack.

quiz.q: What is the first step before setting up an irrigation system?
options: B) Set up the system before planting
quiz.explanation: Setting up irrigation before planting ensures you can water immediately after transplanting.

quiz.q: Which pest cuts cabbage seedlings at ground level?
quiz.explanation: Cutworms sever the stem at the soil line, killing young seedlings.

quiz.q: What is a natural spray to control aphids on cabbage?
options: B) Neem oil or soapy water
quiz.explanation: Neem oil or soapy water sprays are effective and safe for controlling aphids.

quiz.q: What is Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) used for?
options: B) Controlling caterpillars like diamondback moth
quiz.explanation: Bt is a natural bacteria that kills caterpillars without harming beneficial insects.

quiz.q: How can you protect cabbage seedlings from frost?
options: B) Cover with dry grass or plastic tunnels
quiz.explanation: Covering seedlings with dry grass or plastic tunnels at night protects them from frost damage.

quiz.q: What is a good physical barrier to keep insects off cabbage seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Row covers physically exclude insects and birds without chemicals.
